out.reasoning: I anchor on the market’s 27.5% estimate and adjust slightly downward. SD leads the Moderates in all three supplied party-level polls, by 2.5–3.5 percentage points, with only ten days until the election and early voting already underway. The latest Novus poll also shows SD gaining while the Moderates decline. YES most plausibly requires the Moderates to overtake SD while the Social Democrats remain ahead; Sweden’s broadly proportional seat allocation makes vote rankings informative. Nevertheless, correlated polling errors, turnout differences and late campaign shifts leave a meaningful chance of that reversal. The 2022 SD–Moderate gap was also relatively narrow. These considerations support 25%, rather than a large departure from the informed market estimate.

I modestly discount the market’s 0.275 estimate. SD leads the Moderates in all three party-level polls: by 2.5 points in Verian, 3.5 in Novus and 3.4 in Demoskop. With ten days remaining and early voting underway, that consistency favors SD finishing second rather than third. The Social Democrats remain clearly ahead, while other parties are far behind, so YES principally requires the Moderates to overtake SD. Correlated polling error, differential turnout and late campaign shifts make that plausible; the latest Verian lead is not decisive. Broadly proportional seat allocation means vote rankings should usually translate into seat rankings. The evidence supports only a modest downward adjustment from the informed crowd estimate, rather than treating SD’s polling lead as secure.

I give substantial weight to the market’s 27.5% estimate but adjust slightly downward because all three party-level polls place SD second, ahead of the Moderates by 2.5–3.5 percentage points. SD finishing third would most plausibly require the Moderates to overtake it while the Social Democrats remain ahead. With ten days until voting, correlated polling error and late campaign shifts make that plausible, but it is not the central outcome. Proportional seat allocation makes vote rankings a useful guide to seat rankings. Bloc-level polling offers little additional evidence about SD versus the Moderates.

Poll errors across these surveys are not independent, and seat allocation can produce a different ordering from a very close vote-share comparison. If voting and counting proceed normally and current polling rankings persist, SD finishes second and this proposition resolves NO.
